glossary.alphaAnnual: The part of the annual return the market does not explain. This is what a stock picker is actually paid for, and here it is usually small.
glossary.annualisedVolatility: How much the weekly return typically swings, scaled to a year.
glossary.bestWeek: The single best week. Worth seeing next to the CAGR, because one week can carry a year.
glossary.cagr: The steady annual rate that would produce the same ending value. Smooths a bumpy path into one figure.
glossary.calmar: Annual return divided by the worst peak-to-trough fall. Answers: how much do I earn per unit of the pain I have to sit through?
glossary.costDragAnnual: How much trading costs took out per year. A strategy that only works before costs is not a strategy.
glossary.dateConvention: Whether a return stamped at a date means the week ending then or the week following. This repository contains both, and mixing them silently was what produced a withdrawn result in Step 291.
glossary.longestDrawdownWeeks: How long the worst underwater stretch lasted before making a new high. Often harder to live with than the depth.
glossary.marketBeta: How much the book moves for each 1% the market moves. Near 1 means you are mostly holding the market. This is the number that explained most of this project's headline returns.
glossary.marketR2: The share of the book's movement explained by the market alone. High means the strategy is the market wearing a different name.
glossary.maxDrawdown: The worst fall from a high point to the low that followed. The number that decides whether you can actually hold the thing.
glossary.pnlOnNotional: What £10,000 would have become, in money rather than percentages.
glossary.profitFactor: Total gains divided by total losses. Above 1 means the wins outweigh the losses; it pairs with win rate to show whether wins are big or merely frequent.
glossary.sharpe: Return divided by volatility. How much reward per unit of bounce. Above 1 is good, above 2 is rare and usually a sign to check the arithmetic.
glossary.sortino: Like Sharpe but only counts downside moves as risk, since upside volatility is not something anyone complains about.
glossary.timeUnderWater: The share of all weeks spent below a previous peak. A strategy can be profitable and still be underwater most of the time.
glossary.totalReturn: What one pound became over the whole record, before any tax. The simplest honest number.
glossary.turnoverAnnual: How much of the book is replaced per year. High turnover multiplies cost and makes execution assumptions matter.
glossary.winRate: Share of weeks that were positive. High win rates feel good and say almost nothing on their own -- a strategy can win 70% of weeks and still lose money.

readThisFirst: Sharpe, Calmar and win rate describe the shape of a return series. They cannot tell you whether the return came from skill or from holding the market. Market beta and alpha can, and for most strategies here the answer is the market.
